newsitem.title: USA: DLA calls ATPC tin sales complaints a red herring.
newsitem.headline: DLA calls ATPC tin sales complaints a red herring.

text.p: The U.S. Defense Logistics Agency dismissed complaints from the Association of Tin Producing Countries (ATPC) that sales of tin from its stockpile lacked transparency and should be restrained.

Richard Connelly, the DLA's stockpile administrator, said the complaint about lack of transparency was a "red herring", adding that all the spot sales bids are published, along with a provisional price for negotiated long-term sales.
"We are much more transparent than anybody else in the business. I fail to grasp the logic of their statement," Connelly said.
The ATPC, which has been a regular critic of stockpile tin sales, met in Singapore September 23-24. The association has given up its main role in limiting exports for the time being.

Earlier this year at Metal Bulletin's tin conference in Miami, Connelly unveiled plans to change the structure of sales from October 1 by eliminating the daily spot sales. The DLA asked for industry comment.
The ATPC last met DLA officials at the Pentagon in Washington three years ago, Connelly said, and did not submit any comments on the new sales plan from October 1.
The DLA has declined to stop or limit tin sales because it does not believe they disrupt the market.

From October 1 the daily spot sales will be replaced by two long-term contract sales of 5,000 tonnes each in February and July 1997. A further 2,000 tonnes will be sold in a sealed bid process, with a maximum 200 tonnes available each month until the 2,000 tonnes is exhausted.
"For the time being this is our plan and I intend to stick to it," Connelly said.
He reiterated the DLA's undertaking that 12,000 tonnes at most would be sold each year. The stockpile has 120,000 tonnes of Longhorn tin left, enough for ten years of sales.
Western world tin consumption was about 190,000 tonnes last year.
